evidence.paraphrase: After Śukla’s meal, Vināyaka plays outside and briefly sleeps. Citizens who prepared meals seek the sage’s son at the Kāśī king’s house; the king says he left while playing. Some disparage the choice of a poor man’s inferior meal over wealthy invitations and challenge the king’s deity claim. Devotees find him sleeping at Śukla’s house: sāttvika people wait silently, while rājasika people urge him to rise before the prepared food becomes stale and criticize Śukla’s poverty. The child, explicitly called Kaśyapa’s son, says the devotional meal fully satisfied him, leaving no strength to step or appetite for another mouthful. The people become disappointed.

narrative_events.details: Prepared-meal invitations and disparagement of Śukla bring citizens to the sleeping child. He declares the small devotional meal satisfying and refuses another mouthful.

The one Lord becomes many, visiting every home with the king, accepting elaborate hospitality, playing/teaching and fulfilling wishes. Drums and flowers mark the event; the king cannot explain simultaneous visits.
Inspecting two or three homes, the king sees himself and the child after each meal.
Sanaka/Sanandana find the deity everywhere, cannot find a pure meal place and leave hungry. Meditation reveals Vināyaka within, around and in each other.
The ten-armed lion-mounted vision appears. The pair bow and praise, saying their wish is already fulfilled; no fresh personal grant is spoken.
After disappearance, the relieved pair install the as-seen image and name the shrine and lake. Visitors worship and depart; the sages return, followed by conditional account-hearing benefits.
The king’s exhausted house search ends at Śukla’s. His reproach meets the child’s reply and citizens’ testimony; he recognizes the deluding māyā.
Meditation brings Vināyaka-form; māyā restores royal distinction. The child is carried toward the palace in a palanquin.
Seeing the devoted couple follow, the child mentally grants extraordinary wealth without a new spoken request.
The returning couple fear offense and the missing hut, then discover servants, ornaments, palatial dwelling and food. Śukla recognizes unobtrusive grace and teaches the value of devotion.
Hidden lightning-form envoys attack. Bearers flee; the child seizes and whirls the pair, compassionately stops and questions them.
They confess Narāntaka’s mission and praise their rescuer through the five illustrative father roles.
Citizens warn of future harm. The Lord preserves his earlier fearlessness promise and releases the pair; king and child reach home.
The envoys return to Raudrapura and introduce their report with the duty to tell good and bad truthfully.
They recount the earlier demons’ forms, counters and deaths, followed by their own attack and release. Differently printed recap identities remain unresolved.
They report Śukla’s meal and simultaneous royal/deity household visits, then counsel careful self-interest and admit the child’s unmatched power.
Narāntaka rejects caution, threatens child/king and orders the four-division host to arm for Kāśī.
The equipped divisions march with frightening dust and noise; an unnamed minister rides a jeweled chariot. Gods flee to a cave as Narāntaka approaches.
The king arms, seeks counsel and hears conditional surrender/delivery advice, which is not implemented.
Demons burn the city and capture/assault fleeing inhabitants. The king chooses fighting rather than tolerating abduction.
After initial success, the king and two ministers’ sons are captured alive. Narāntaka boasts that the child must now be defeated and marches home.
Ambā faints and laments her captured husband; widowhood language remains her despairing speech.
The child roars at the grief and Siddhi creates the terrifying host in response to his war purpose.
The leader asks food; the Lord orders consumption of the army and bringing Narāntaka’s head, promising more food if needed.
Kālapuruṣa consumes all divisions, counters arrows/astras and exhausts the demon’s weapons, then pursues him through the worlds.
Seized by the hair, the living demon is forcibly brought before Vināyaka with refuge advice; no actual surrender is narrated.
The leader asks rest and the demon’s liberation. The explicit answer grants rest in the mouth; the leader enters and is reabsorbed. Demon liberation remains ungranted in this speech.
Brahmā explains the leader through Vināyaka’s universal creative power, retaining Siddhi’s proximate agency.
The captives see worlds/universes in the belly, seek mental refuge and leave by the child-shown hair-pore route.
The king recalls capture and rescue and asks its causes. A head touch gives divine knowledge; after his hymn the Lord again veils it through māyā.
The king reunites with his unnamed mother and then wife Ambā; the companion label shifts to ministers without secure identity allocation. The population is restored and families celebrate.

variants_and_conflicts.description: 25 and54 report Sanaka/Sanandana’s universal sight and installation.54.59 prints vararado and names Gaṇeśatīrtha versus25 Varada/Gaṇeśakuṇḍa. Preserve source-order reports and do not assert a new physical identity or chronological equation.

23 reports an explicit request/grant and wealth, but55.18 says the child had not yet given a pleasing boon and55.19 narrates a mental gift. Both report contexts retained without deleting or harmonizing the earlier grant.

The Capala of10.1–17 is explicitly killed by consecrated rice, whereas Capala55 is seized, released and reports back56. Distinct provisional source-local actors retained; no resurrection or identical-person equation invented.

56.9–16 printed prabala/kuṇḍiyāstuvaraḥ/Jṛmbhiṇī/Jvālāsura/Vyāghratuṇḍa/Vidāraṇa/Megha differ from earlier Kūṭa/Kuṇḍa/Jṛmbhā/Jvālāmukha/Vyāghramukha/Dāruṇa/Hemajjyotirvid. Source-specific forms/counters preserved; exact segmentation and identities need collation.

57.41–43/59.7/9 identifies two ministers’ sons captured with the king;59.39 calls the pair amātyau. Keep exact role labels without inventing a fathers’ return or silently changing the sons into ministers.
